c.tagline: A palm-fringed diving gateway on one of Africa's largest natural bays.

taxi.fareNote: There are no ride-hail apps in Pemba — agree the fare with the driver before setting off. Shared chapas (minibuses) are the cheapest way around, with taxis and tuk-tuks for short hops.

emergency.note: 112 works from mobile phones and connects to emergency services; landline numbers are 119 (police), 117 (ambulance) and 198 (fire).

avoid.reason: Cabo Delgado province — insurgency in the north; check advisories, avoid northern districts

hood_desc: The palm-lined main beach strip on the bay's ocean side, home to most of the resorts, dive centres, beach bars and seafood restaurants; the base most visitors choose for sun, snorkelling and diving.
The commercial and administrative heart of Pemba around Avenida 25 de Setembro and the market, with banks, shops, government offices and the airport road; the practical town centre.
The old lower town beside the harbour on the bay, with the port, dhow anchorage, fish market and faded Portuguese-era buildings; the working, historic waterfront of the city.

The dense, lively neighbourhood behind the town centre where much of Pemba's population lives, with busy street markets, chapa ranks and local eateries; an authentic, budget-friendly slice of the city.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water only.

transit.hours: Chapas run from around dawn until early evening; after dark, taxis and tuk-tuks are the main way to get around.
transit.note: Pemba has no formal public transport system; getting around means shared chapas (converted minibuses) along the main roads, plus taxis and tuk-tuks for door-to-door and beach runs.
transit.pay: Pay the chapa conductor in cash (roughly 15-25 meticais a hop); taxi and tuk-tuk fares are negotiated and paid in cash. Carry small notes.

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or leaving ~10% at tourist restaurants and for dive/tour guides is appreciated where service isn't already added.

landmarks: Wimbe Beach
Pemba's palm-fringed showpiece, a long arc of pale sand and warm Indian Ocean water lined with breezy seafood restaurants and dhow silhouettes.
Paquitequete Fishing Village
The town's historic Swahili quarter on a sandy spit, where brightly painted dhows land the day's catch amid coral-stone houses and drying nets.
Pemba Bay
One of the world's largest natural harbors, a vast sheltered bay best savored on a sunset dhow cruise with the town lights twinkling ashore.
Pemba Old Town (Baixa)
The faded Portuguese colonial downtown near the port, where pastel art-deco facades and old trading houses recall the city's days as Porto Amélia.
Artes Maconde Craft Cooperative
A renowned workshop where Makonde carvers shape ebony and blackwood into intricate 'family tree' sculptures, masks and jewelry sold at fair prices.
Chuiba Beach
A quieter ribbon of white sand beyond Wimbe, backed by coconut palms and simple beach lodges, ideal for long solitary walks.
Murrébuè Beach
A wind-blessed beach south of town that has become northern Mozambique's kitesurfing hub, with mangroves, tidal flats and reliable cross-shore breezes.
Quirimbas Archipelago & National Park
A pristine chain of coral islands north of Pemba, protected as a national park, offering world-class diving, mangrove channels and Robinson Crusoe sandbanks.
Ibo Island & Fort São João Baptista
A hauntingly beautiful former Portuguese trading post in the Quirimbas, where silversmiths work inside a star-shaped 18th-century fort draped in bougainvillea.
Mercado Municipal de Pemba
The town's bustling central market, piled with cassava, capulana cloth, spices and reef fish, the liveliest window onto everyday Pemba life.

train.note: Cabo Delgado has no railway and none has ever reached Pemba. The nearest track is the Nacala corridor several hundred kilometres to the south, where CFM and the Nacala concession run a slow passenger train between Nampula and Cuamba with an onward service to Lichinga (https://www.cfm.co.mz/); reaching it from Pemba means a full day on the road. Nothing crosses the Rovuma into Tanzania by rail. Pemba is realistically reached by air or by long-distance bus.

bus.note: Buses and chapas leave the Pemba bus stand near the market very early, usually 04:00-05:00, for Nampula over the EN106/EN1 in around 7-9 hours, with onward connections there to Beira and Maputo; Nagi Investimentos and Maning Nice run the main long-haul coaches and tickets are bought at the yard the day before. Local chapas serve Wimbe beach, Metuge and Mecufi. There are no scheduled international coaches - the Unity Bridge crossing to Tanzania at Negomano and the coast road north through Mocimboa da Praia have been affected by the Cabo Delgado insurgency and are not a practical or safe route, so check current government travel advice before any overland journey north or west of Pemba.

ferry.note: Pemba sits on one of the world's largest natural harbours, but the port handles cargo and gas-project traffic and there are no scheduled passenger ships. Boats to the Quirimbas islands are dhows and lodge speedboats rather than timetabled ferries; the usual jumping-off point for Ibo is Tandanhangue near Quissanga, and dhow crossings depend on the tide and can take two to four hours, while a lodge speedboat does it in well under an hour. Small local boats cross Pemba Bay from Paquitequete. There are no international sailings, and access to the northern islands has been intermittently restricted for security reasons.
